questions.questionText: Your team needs to provision a Compute Engine virtual machine for a legacy application that requires exactly 12 vCPUs and 40 GB of RAM. Choosing a standard predefined machine type would result in over-provisioning and wasted costs. How should you provision this specific compute resource?
options: Provision an App Engine Flexible instance.
Create a Compute Engine instance using a Custom Machine Type.
Provision a smaller predefined VM and enable CPU bursting.
Deploy the application on Cloud Run and set memory limits.
correctAnswers: Create a Compute Engine instance using a Custom Machine Type.

explanation.general explanation: Compute Engine allows you to create Custom Machine Types, where you can independently specify the exact number of vCPUs and the amount of memory your workload requires. This ensures you only provision and pay for the exact compute resources needed.

why other options are wrong.Provision an App Engine Flexible instanc: App Engine Flexible does not allow granular vCPU to RAM ratio customizations in the exact way Custom Machine Types do for IaaS workloads.
why other options are wrong.Provision a smaller predefined VM and en: Standard Compute Engine instances do not support arbitrary 'bursting' to completely different vCPU/RAM limits beyond their provisioned capacity.
why other options are wrong.Deploy the application on Cloud Run and: Cloud Run has maximum CPU/Memory limits that are smaller than 12 vCPUs and 40 GB RAM, and it is a container service, not a raw VM replacement.

questions.questionText: You are provisioning compute resources for a large batch processing job. The job is highly fault-tolerant and can resume from checkpoints if a server is shut down unexpectedly. To minimize provisioning costs, which Compute Engine feature should you use?

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs (formerly preemptible VMs) are highly discounted compute instances that Google Cloud can reclaim at any time. Because the workload is fault-tolerant and can survive sudden shutdowns, Spot VMs are the perfect provisioning choice for maximizing cost savings.

why other options are wrong.Sole-tenant nodes: Sole-tenant nodes provide dedicated hardware, which increases costs and is used for compliance or BYOL, not cost savings.
why other options are wrong.Shielded VMs: Shielded VMs provide verifiable integrity against rootkits; they do not provide cost discounts.
why other options are wrong.Committed use discounts: CUDs are for predictable, continuous, long-term workloads, whereas batch processing is typically temporary and better suited for Spot pricing.

questions.questionText: You want to provision a fleet of identical web servers that can automatically scale in and out based on CPU utilization. Which Google Cloud resource must you create first to define the configuration of the VMs before provisioning the autoscaling group?

explanation.general explanation: Before you can provision a Managed Instance Group (MIG) that autoscales, you must create an Instance Template. The Instance Template defines the machine type, boot disk image, labels, and startup scripts that the MIG will use to provision identical, standardized VMs.

why other options are wrong.A Managed Instance Group (MIG): The MIG is the group itself; it requires an Instance Template to be created first so it knows what kind of VMs to provision.
why other options are wrong.A Cloud Load Balancer: A load balancer distributes traffic to the VMs, but it does not define the VM configurations.
why other options are wrong.A Cloud Router: A Cloud Router handles dynamic BGP routing for hybrid networks, not VM provisioning.

questions.questionText: Your organization wants to provision a Kubernetes environment to run containerized microservices. The operations team has strictly stated they do not want to provision, manage, or patch the underlying worker node virtual machines. Which service should you provision?

explanation.general explanation: GKE Autopilot is a mode of operations in GKE where Google fully manages the entire cluster's infrastructure, including provisioning, patching, and scaling the underlying worker nodes. You only interact with the Kubernetes API to deploy your pods.

why other options are wrong.Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Standard: In GKE Standard, you are responsible for configuring, managing, and provisioning the node pools (the underlying VMs).
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine Managed Instance Groups: MIGs require you to manage the underlying VMs completely.
why other options are wrong.App Engine Flexible: App Engine Flex is a PaaS that uses containers, but it is not a Kubernetes environment.

questions.questionText: Sole-tenant nodes are dedicated physical Compute Engine servers for your project. Which two scenarios are valid reasons to provision Sole-tenant nodes instead of standard multi-tenant VMs? (Choose two)
options: To satisfy strict compliance requirements that mandate physical hardware isolation.
To bring your own licenses (BYOL) that require licensing per physical core.
To achieve the absolute lowest cost per minute for burstable web traffic.
To completely eliminate the need to patch the guest operating systems.
To automatically run Apache Spark clusters without manual setup.
correctAnswers: To satisfy strict compliance requirements that mandate physical hardware isolation.
To bring your own licenses (BYOL) that require licensing per physical core.

explanation.general explanation: Sole-tenant nodes guarantee that only your VMs run on a specific physical server. This is primarily used for strict hardware-level isolation for compliance, or to map software licenses (BYOL like Windows/SQL Server) to physical cores rather than virtual cores.

why other options are wrong.To achieve the absolute lowest cost per: Sole-tenant nodes are generally more expensive because you pay for the entire physical server, making them unsuitable for cheap, burstable workloads.
why other options are wrong.To completely eliminate the need to patc: Sole-tenant nodes are still IaaS; you must patch the guest OS yourself.
why other options are wrong.To automatically run Apache Spark cluste: This describes Cloud Dataproc, not Sole-tenant nodes.

questions.questionText: A developer has written a stateless web application packaged as a Docker container. They want to provision it in a fully managed serverless environment that charges only when requests are being processed and automatically scales to zero. Which service should they choose?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Run is a fully managed, serverless compute platform specifically designed for deploying stateless HTTP containers. It scales out automatically upon receiving requests and natively scales to zero when idle.

why other options are wrong.App Engine Standard: App Engine Standard runs source code directly in predefined runtimes, not custom Docker containers (which require App Engine Flexible, and Flex cannot scale to zero).
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine: VMs do not scale to zero automatically without complex custom engineering, and they bill continuously.
why other options are wrong.Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Standard: GKE requires you to pay for minimum running nodes, meaning it does not scale the infrastructure cost to zero.

questions.questionText: Your company mandates that all Google Cloud infrastructure must be provisioned via code to ensure repeatability, version control, and audibility. Which declarative Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool is the Google-recommended standard for provisioning GCP resources?

explanation.general explanation: Terraform by HashiCorp is the industry and Google-recommended declarative Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool for provisioning and managing Google Cloud resources. Google actively maintains the official Terraform provider for GCP.

why other options are wrong.Ansible: While Ansible can provision infrastructure, it is primarily an imperative configuration management tool (setting up the OS/software), not the primary declarative IaC tool for GCP infrastructure provisioning.
why other options are wrong.Chef: Chef is a configuration management tool focused on server configuration.
why other options are wrong.Puppet: Puppet is a configuration management tool focused on server configuration.

questions.questionText: You are provisioning a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. Your application has two distinct components: a web frontend that requires standard CPUs, and a machine learning model that strictly requires NVIDIA GPUs. How should you provision the compute resources in the cluster to support this?
options: Provision two separate node pools: one with standard VMs and one with GPU-enabled VMs.
Provision a single node pool and install the GPU drivers manually on half the VMs.
Attach GPUs to the GKE Control Plane.
Deploy the frontend to Cloud Run and the ML model to GKE.
correctAnswers: Provision two separate node pools: one with standard VMs and one with GPU-enabled VMs.

explanation.general explanation: In GKE, a node pool is a group of nodes within a cluster that all have the same configuration. To run workloads with different hardware requirements (like standard CPUs vs GPUs) in the same cluster, you provision multiple node pools, each tailored to specific hardware needs.

why other options are wrong.Provision a single node pool and install: Node pools enforce identical configurations on all nodes within the pool; you cannot manually modify half the nodes in a managed pool.
The GKE control plane is fully managed by Google and you cannot attach GPUs to it.
why other options are wrong.Deploy the frontend to Cloud Run and the: While possible architecturally, the question specifically asks how to provision the compute resources *in the cluster* to support this.

questions.questionText: A developer has written a web application in standard Python 3.9. They want a fully managed provisioning experience where they simply push their source code, and the platform handles all infrastructure, routing, and scaling down to zero. Which service natively fits this requirement?

explanation.general explanation: App Engine Standard allows developers to deploy source code (like Python, Java, Node.js) directly to predefined, fully managed runtimes. It handles all underlying infrastructure provisioning and natively supports scaling to zero.

why other options are wrong.App Engine Flexible: App Engine Flexible is used for custom docker containers, and it does not scale to zero (it requires at least one instance running).
why other options are wrong.Cloud Run: Cloud Run requires the developer to build and push a Docker container image, whereas the requirement is to simply push source code.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine: Compute Engine is IaaS and requires complete manual provisioning of the OS, runtime, and scaling infrastructure.

questions.questionText: When provisioning a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) environment, you can configure autoscalers to dynamically adjust compute resources. Which two autoscaling mechanisms are native to GKE for scaling node infrastructure and pod replicas? (Choose two)

explanation.general explanation: In GKE, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) dynamically scales the number of pod replicas based on metrics like CPU utilization. If the pods cannot be scheduled due to lack of node capacity, the Cluster Autoscaler automatically provisions new underlying worker nodes.

why other options are wrong.Managed Instance Group Autoscaler: While GKE node pools use MIGs under the hood, you configure the 'Cluster Autoscaler' in GKE, not the raw MIG autoscaler.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Run Concurrency Autoscaler: This is specific to Cloud Run, not GKE.
why other options are wrong.App Engine Dynamic Autoscaler: This is specific to App Engine, not GKE.

questions.questionText: You have provisioned a group of VMs to run a legacy monolithic application. Occasionally, the application process crashes or hangs, making the VM unresponsive on port 80. You want Google Cloud to automatically recreate the VM if the application stops responding. What should you configure?
options: A Managed Instance Group (MIG) with Autohealing and an HTTP health check.
An Unmanaged Instance Group with a Cloud Load Balancer.
A Cloud Monitoring alert linked to a Cloud Function.
A startup script on the VM that checks for port 80.
correctAnswers: A Managed Instance Group (MIG) with Autohealing and an HTTP health check.

explanation.general explanation: Autohealing is a feature of Managed Instance Groups (MIGs). By attaching an application-based health check (like checking port 80), the MIG continuously monitors the VM. If the application stops responding, the MIG automatically deletes the unhealthy VM and provisions a new one from the instance template.

why other options are wrong.An Unmanaged Instance Group with a Cloud: Load balancers stop sending traffic to unhealthy VMs, but they do not recreate or reboot them.
why other options are wrong.A Cloud Monitoring alert linked to a Clo: While possible to script custom automation, MIG Autohealing is a native, out-of-the-box feature designed exactly for this.
why other options are wrong.A startup script on the VM that checks f: A startup script only runs once when the VM boots; it does not continuously monitor application health.

questions.questionText: Your team needs to provision a lightweight Node.js script that runs instantly every time a user uploads an image to a specific Cloud Storage bucket. The script resizes the image and saves it. Which serverless compute service is the best fit for provisioning this event-driven code?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Functions is an event-driven, serverless compute service. It natively integrates with Cloud Storage events (like file uploads), allowing you to run a single-purpose script (like image resizing) without provisioning any infrastructure.

why other options are wrong.App Engine Standard: App Engine is designed for full web applications responding to HTTP requests, not lightweight scripts triggered by Cloud Storage events.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine: Provisioning a VM just to wait for image uploads is expensive and adds unnecessary OS management overhead.
why other options are wrong.Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE): Provisioning a Kubernetes cluster for a simple event-driven script is massive operational overkill.

questions.questionText: Your company handles highly sensitive intellectual property. Security policies mandate that data must be encrypted not only at rest and in transit, but also while it is actively being processed in system memory (RAM). Which Compute Engine feature must you provision to meet this requirement?

explanation.general explanation: Confidential VMs use specialized hardware (AMD EPYC processors with SEV) to encrypt data while it is in use in the system memory (RAM). This ensures that even if the hypervisor was compromised, the data in memory remains secure.

why other options are wrong.Shielded VMs: Shielded VMs protect against rootkits and boot-level malware using secure boot and vTPM; they do not encrypt data in RAM.
why other options are wrong.Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys (CSEK): CSEK is used for encrypting data at rest (Persistent Disks), not data in memory.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Key Management Service (KMS): KMS manages encryption keys for data at rest, not for real-time hardware-level memory encryption.

questions.questionText: You are provisioning a Compute Engine virtual machine to train a machine learning model. The training software heavily relies on hardware acceleration. How do you provide this hardware acceleration to the VM?
options: Attach NVIDIA GPUs to the VM during provisioning.
Enable the 'Compute Optimized' flag on the VM.
Provision a memory-optimized M2 machine type.
Attach an SSD Persistent Disk configured for high IOPS.
correctAnswers: Attach NVIDIA GPUs to the VM during provisioning.

explanation.general explanation: Compute Engine allows you to attach hardware accelerators, specifically NVIDIA GPUs (Graphics Processing Units), to your virtual machines. These are essential for highly parallel processing tasks like training machine learning models.

why other options are wrong.Enable the 'Compute Optimized' flag on t: Compute-optimized (C2) VMs offer high CPU performance, but they do not provide the massive parallel acceleration of dedicated hardware GPUs required for ML.
why other options are wrong.Provision a memory-optimized M2 machine: M2 machines provide massive RAM (e.g., for SAP HANA), not hardware acceleration for ML.
why other options are wrong.Attach an SSD Persistent Disk configured: SSDs accelerate storage I/O, not compute/math calculations for machine learning.

questions.questionText: When provisioning Spot VMs (which replaced preemptible VMs) for fault-tolerant workloads on Google Cloud, what are two fundamental characteristics of these resources? (Choose two)
options: They are offered at significantly lower prices compared to standard VMs.
Google Compute Engine can terminate them at any time to reclaim capacity.
They automatically restart with the exact same internal state after termination.
They are exclusively reserved for machine learning workloads.
They provide a guaranteed 24-hour runtime before being preempted.
correctAnswers: They are offered at significantly lower prices compared to standard VMs.
Google Compute Engine can terminate them at any time to reclaim capacity.

explanation.general explanation: Spot VMs use excess Google Cloud capacity and are offered at a steep discount (up to 91%). The trade-off is that Google can terminate (preempt) these VMs at any time if it needs the capacity back for standard VMs.

why other options are wrong.They automatically restart with the exac: Spot VMs lose their internal memory state when preempted. You must design workloads to checkpoint data externally.
why other options are wrong.They are exclusively reserved for machin: Spot VMs can be used for any fault-tolerant workload (batch, rendering, CI/CD), not just ML.
why other options are wrong.They provide a guaranteed 24-hour runtim: Classic Preemptible VMs had a maximum 24-hour runtime, but Spot VMs do not have a maximum runtime limit; however, they still have NO guarantee and can be preempted at any minute.

questions.questionText: You are migrating a monolithic web application that relies on custom OS-level dependencies and background threads that sometimes run for 30 minutes. You want to use a managed Platform as a Service (PaaS) on Google Cloud where you provide a custom Docker container. Which service must you provision?

explanation.general explanation: App Engine Flexible is a managed PaaS that allows you to provide custom Docker runtimes. Crucially, because it runs on Compute Engine VMs under the hood, it supports long-running background processes (request timeouts up to 24 hours), making it suitable for this legacy monolithic app.

why other options are wrong.App Engine Standard: App Engine Standard uses predefined runtimes (no custom Docker) and has strict request timeouts (usually 60 seconds to 10 minutes depending on scaling mode).
why other options are wrong.Cloud Functions: Cloud Functions is for short-lived snippets (max 9 mins for 1st gen, 60 mins for 2nd gen) and is not a PaaS for monolithic web apps.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Run: Cloud Run does accept Docker containers, but it is optimized for stateless HTTP handling and currently limits request timeouts to 60 minutes, which might not be ideal for deep OS-level background thread dependencies compared to App Engine Flex.

questions.questionText: You are provisioning a high-traffic web API using Cloud Run. You want to optimize costs by processing as many HTTP requests as possible simultaneously within a single container instance before scaling out to new instances. Which provisioning setting should you adjust?

explanation.general explanation: In Cloud Run, 'Maximum Concurrency' defines the maximum number of requests that can be processed simultaneously by a given container instance. Increasing this allows a single container to handle multiple overlapping requests, reducing the total number of instances provisioned and optimizing costs.

why other options are wrong.CPU Allocation: While increasing CPU might be necessary to support higher concurrency, it does not explicitly define how many requests the container is allowed to take simultaneously.
why other options are wrong.Memory Limit: Memory limits define how much RAM the container can use, not the request concurrency limit.
why other options are wrong.Execution Environment: The execution environment defines whether you use first-gen or second-gen infrastructure, not concurrency limits.

questions.questionText: Your application is hosted on a Regional Managed Instance Group (MIG). You need to provision a new version of the application by updating the underlying OS image without causing downtime. What is the Google-recommended approach to provision this update?
options: Perform a Rolling Update on the MIG with the new Instance Template.
SSH into each VM and manually update the OS packages.
Delete the MIG and recreate it with the new Instance Template.
Use Live Migration to patch the VMs while they are running.
correctAnswers: Perform a Rolling Update on the MIG with the new Instance Template.

explanation.general explanation: MIGs support an Automated Rolling Update feature. You supply a new Instance Template, and the MIG will incrementally provision new VMs and delete old ones based on your specified surge parameters, ensuring the application remains available with zero downtime.

why other options are wrong.SSH into each VM and manually update the: MIGs are designed to be immutable; manually patching them is an anti-pattern. If autoscaling occurs, new VMs will boot with the old image.
why other options are wrong.Delete the MIG and recreate it with the: Deleting the MIG causes immediate downtime.
why other options are wrong.Use Live Migration to patch the VMs whil: Live Migration is a Google infrastructure feature used to move VMs during host maintenance without downtime; it is not a tool for users to deploy new application/OS versions.

questions.questionText: When provisioning new Compute Engine virtual machines from a standard Google-provided OS image, you want to automatically install a web server and download application code the very first time the VM boots up. What feature should you use?

explanation.general explanation: Startup scripts in Compute Engine allow you to specify code or scripts that automatically execute during the boot process of a virtual machine. This is the standard way to perform automated software installation and configuration immediately after a VM is provisioned.

why other options are wrong.OS Patch Management: Patch management is for applying security updates to existing OS installations, not for initial application bootstrapping.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Build Triggers: Cloud Build is a CI/CD platform for building containers or artifacts, not a VM configuration agent.
why other options are wrong.Google Cloud Deployment Manager: Deployment Manager provisions the infrastructure (the VM itself), but you still pass a startup script to it to handle the in-OS software installation.

questions.questionText: When provisioning a Cloud Function, you have several configuration options that dictate its execution environment and costs. Which two parameters are explicitly configured by the user during the provisioning of a Cloud Function? (Choose two)

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Functions is a fully managed serverless environment. When provisioning a function, the user must define the 'Memory allocation' (which also proportionally scales the CPU) and the 'Timeout duration' (how long the function is allowed to run before being terminated).

why other options are wrong.Operating System version (e.g., Ubuntu 2: The OS is completely abstracted and managed by Google; the user only selects a language runtime (like Node.js 18).
why other options are wrong.Underlying Virtual Machine type (e.g., e: The underlying VMs are hidden from the user in serverless environments.
why other options are wrong.Container orchestration engine (e.g., Ku: Cloud Functions abstracts away all orchestration; the user provides raw code.

questions.questionText: Your organization wants to provision an application on Compute Engine that can survive the total failure of a single Google Cloud zone (e.g., us-central1-a). Which provisioning architecture provides this high availability?
options: An Unmanaged Instance Group spanning multiple regions.

explanation.general explanation: A Regional Managed Instance Group automatically provisions and balances VMs across multiple zones within a single region (e.g., us-central1-a, us-central1-b, us-central1-c). If one zone goes down, the MIG automatically provisions new VMs in the healthy zones to maintain availability.

A Zonal MIG lives entirely within one zone; if that zone fails, the entire group goes offline.
why other options are wrong.An Unmanaged Instance Group spanning mul: Unmanaged instance groups do not support automatic scaling, autohealing, or automatic cross-zone balancing.
A single node represents a single point of failure within a single zone.

questions.questionText: You are provisioning a Kubernetes cluster. You want Google Cloud to manage the highly available control plane (master nodes) automatically, but you want complete administrative control (SSH access) over the provisioning and management of the underlying worker node virtual machines. Which mode of GKE should you choose?

explanation.general explanation: In GKE Standard mode, Google manages the Kubernetes control plane for you, but you retain full control over provisioning the node pools. You can SSH into the worker nodes, configure custom instance types, and manage the underlying VMs.

why other options are wrong.GKE Autopilot: In Autopilot mode, Google manages both the control plane AND the worker nodes. You do not have SSH access to the underlying nodes.
why other options are wrong.Anthos Service Mesh: This is a service mesh for managing microservice communications, not a Kubernetes cluster provisioning mode.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine with MicroK8s: In this scenario, you would have to manually manage both the control plane AND the worker nodes, which violates the requirement.

questions.questionText: Security compliance requires that all provisioned VMs must cryptographically verify that their boot sequence and kernel have not been tampered with by malware or rootkits. Which specific VM type must you provision to enable Secure Boot and Virtual Trusted Platform Module (vTPM)?

explanation.general explanation: Shielded VMs are hardened virtual machines on Google Cloud. They offer features like Secure Boot, vTPM (Virtual Trusted Platform Module), and Integrity Monitoring to defend against rootkits and boot-level malware.

why other options are wrong.Confidential VMs: Confidential VMs encrypt data in use (RAM) while the VM is running; they focus on in-memory encryption, whereas Shielded VMs focus on boot-level integrity.
why other options are wrong.Spot VMs: Spot VMs are cheap, preemptible instances. They can be Shielded VMs, but 'Spot' itself does not denote the security features.
why other options are wrong.Sole-tenant nodes: These provide dedicated physical hardware isolation, not cryptographic secure boot verification natively.

questions.questionText: Your company has thousands of virtual machines running on an on-premises VMware vSphere environment. You need to provision a cloud environment that allows you to migrate these VMs directly to Google Cloud quickly without converting the VM formats or changing your IP subnets. Which service should you provision?

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud VMware Engine provides a fully managed VMware vSphere environment running natively on Google Cloud bare metal infrastructure. This allows organizations to execute a rapid 'lift and shift' of their existing VMware workloads without re-architecting, converting VMs, or changing network topologies.

why other options are wrong.Compute Engine Custom Images: Migrating to standard Compute Engine would require a conversion process from VMware format to Google Compute Engine format.
why other options are wrong.Google Kubernetes Engine: GKE runs containers. Migrating here would require fully refactoring the VMs into Docker containers.
why other options are wrong.Bare Metal Solution: Bare Metal Solution provides raw physical servers primarily for legacy Oracle databases, not a managed VMware environment.

questions.questionText: To provision a highly available, autoscaling web tier using Compute Engine, several components must be configured together. Which two components are strictly required to create an autoscaling Managed Instance Group (MIG)? (Choose two)

explanation.general explanation: To successfully provision an autoscaling Managed Instance Group, you must have an 'Instance Template' (which acts as the blueprint for creating new VMs) and an 'Autoscaling Policy' (which dictates when the MIG should add or remove VMs based on metrics like CPU utilization).

why other options are wrong.Cloud Storage bucket: A storage bucket is not required to provision a MIG.
why other options are wrong.Sole-tenant node: MIGs can run on standard shared infrastructure; sole-tenant nodes are not required.
why other options are wrong.Cloud CDN: While Cloud CDN can cache content from a load balancer in front of a MIG, it is an optional networking component, not a requirement to create the MIG itself.

questions.questionText: Your team uses Terraform to provision infrastructure in Google Cloud. Multiple engineers are collaborating on the code. To prevent conflicts and state corruption, you need to store the Terraform state file securely in a central location that supports locking. What is the recommended Google Cloud service to store the Terraform state?

explanation.general explanation: The Google Cloud recommended best practice for collaborating with Terraform is to configure a backend that stores the Terraform state file in a Cloud Storage bucket. Cloud Storage natively supports state locking and versioning, ensuring safe multi-user collaboration.

why other options are wrong.Cloud SQL: While some databases can be used as backends, Cloud Storage is the native, serverless, and Google-recommended standard for GCP.
why other options are wrong.Firestore: Firestore is a NoSQL document database, not the standard backend for Terraform state.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine Persistent Disk: A persistent disk is block storage attached to a single VM, which makes it useless as a centralized, easily accessible state store for multiple developers.

questions.questionText: In a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) environment, application traffic spikes significantly. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler provisions new Pods, but they are marked as 'Pending' because all worker nodes are currently full. Which GKE feature must be provisioned to automatically add more worker nodes to resolve this?

explanation.general explanation: The Cluster Autoscaler automatically resizes the underlying node pools in a GKE cluster. When it detects that Pods are stuck in a 'Pending' state due to insufficient CPU or memory capacity on existing nodes, it provisions new worker nodes to accommodate them.

why other options are wrong.Node Auto-provisioning: This is an advanced feature of Cluster Autoscaler that creates entirely new node pools, but the primary mechanism simply adding nodes to an existing pool is the Cluster Autoscaler.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine MIG Autoscaler: While GKE uses MIGs under the hood, you do not directly configure the Compute Engine MIG Autoscaler for Kubernetes; you must use the Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler.
why other options are wrong.Vertical Pod Autoscaler: The VPA adjusts the CPU/Memory requests of the pods themselves, not the number of underlying worker nodes.

questions.questionText: You need to provision a serverless environment to run an array of 5,000 independent data processing scripts. Each script is packaged as a Docker container, runs to completion, does not listen for HTTP requests, and takes about 15 minutes to execute. Which service should you choose?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Run Jobs is designed explicitly to execute containerized scripts or batch jobs that run to completion, rather than serving continuous web traffic. It can easily provision and run thousands of parallel array tasks in a fully managed, serverless manner.

why other options are wrong.Cloud Functions: Cloud Functions has execution timeouts and is optimized for event-driven snippets, not orchestrating 5,000 long-running containerized batch tasks.
why other options are wrong.App Engine Standard: App Engine handles HTTP requests; it does not natively run background containerized batch jobs.
why other options are wrong.Compute Engine: Compute Engine would require manual provisioning of VMs, orchestration, and scaling, which violates the requirement for a 'serverless environment'.

questions.questionText: Your team needs to provision a virtual machine to run a massive in-memory database (like SAP HANA). The workload requires up to 12 TB of RAM on a single instance. Which Compute Engine machine family is specifically engineered and provisioned for this type of workload?

explanation.general explanation: The Memory-optimized machine family (like M2 and M3 instances) offers the highest memory-to-vCPU ratio in Google Cloud. They are specifically provisioned for massive in-memory databases like SAP HANA and in-memory analytics workloads.

why other options are wrong.Compute-optimized (C-series): These are optimized for high-performance computing (HPC) and CPU-bound workloads, lacking the massive RAM required.
why other options are wrong.General-purpose (E2-series): These provide a balance of price and performance but top out at far lower memory limits than 12 TB.
why other options are wrong.Accelerator-optimized (A-series): These are designed for massively parallel GPU workloads (Machine Learning/AI), not massive in-memory databases.

questions.questionText: Google Cloud offers various compute services. To minimize operational overhead, the CTO has mandated the use of 'Serverless' technologies wherever possible. Which two compute services are considered fully serverless, meaning you do not provision or manage underlying OS instances or node clusters? (Choose two)

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Run and Cloud Functions are fully managed, serverless compute offerings. They completely abstract the underlying infrastructure, meaning developers do not provision VMs, manage operating systems, or configure node scaling. You only deploy code or containers, and Google handles the rest.

why other options are wrong.Compute Engine: Compute Engine is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS). You must provision and manage the VMs and OS yourself.
why other options are wrong.Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Standard: In GKE Standard, you are responsible for provisioning and managing the underlying node pools.
why other options are wrong.Bare Metal Solution: Bare Metal provides raw physical servers requiring complete manual provisioning and management.
